title: How to Slice Potatoes Restaurant‑Thin with a Mandoline Slicer

html:
Getting potatoes so thin they practically melt in the mouth is easier than you think once you master the mandoline. In this guide we’ll walk through how to slice potatoes thin with mandoline precision, from choosing the right blade to mastering the hand guard. The result? restaurant‑thin, even slices that look impressive on the plate and cook uniformly.

Pick the Right Mandoline Settings

The first step in achieving ultra‑thin potatoes is selecting the proper slice thickness on your Mandoline Slicer. Most adjustable mandolines have a range from 1 mm to 5 mm; for restaurant‑thin slices aim for the 1 mm to 2 mm setting. The thinner the cut, the quicker the potato will crisp up, whether you’re making chips, gratins, or a layered potato casserole.

Prepare the Potato Properly

Before you even bring the mandoline to the counter, prep the potato to make slicing smooth and safe.

  • Wash and peel – A clean, peeled potato reduces friction and prevents the blade from catching on skin.
  • Dry thoroughly – Moisture can cause the potato to slip; pat it dry with a kitchen towel.
  • Trim the ends – Cut off a thin slice from each end to create flat surfaces. This stabilizes the potato when you place it on the mandoline.

With the potato trimmed, you can rest assured that it will sit flat on the mandoline’s platform, giving you consistent thickness from end to end.

Use the Hand Guard – Safety First

The most common mistake when slicing potatoes thin with mandoline is neglecting the hand guard. This little piece of plastic or metal does more than protect your fingers; it also guides the potato straight through the blade, ensuring each slice is even.

Slide the guard onto the potato, hold it firmly, and push the potato down the length of the mandoline using a smooth, steady motion. If you feel any resistance, stop and adjust the guard’s position before continuing. The guard’s ergonomic design reduces wrist strain, which is especially helpful when you’re making a large batch for a dinner party.

Slice Technique for Uniform Cuts

Even the best mandoline won’t produce perfectly thin slices if your technique is off. Follow these steps for a flawless result:

  1. Place the trimmed potato on the mandoline platform, flat side down.
  2. Secure the hand guard over the potato, making sure it covers the entire length.
  3. Grip the guard with one hand and use your other hand to guide the potato toward the blade. Apply gentle, even pressure—don’t force it.
  4. As the potato slides, the blade will cut a thin slice that drops into the collection tray. Keep the motion continuous; stopping and starting creates uneven thickness.
  5. When you reach the end, lift the guard, and use a spatula to retrieve the slices.

With practice, you’ll notice the slices becoming uniformly thin, almost translucent, perfect for crisping up in a hot pan or oven.

Finishing Touches – Cooking Your Thin Slices

Now that you’ve mastered how to slice potatoes thin with mandoline, it’s time to put them to use. Here are three quick ways to finish them:

  • Pan‑Fry – Heat a thin layer of oil in a skillet, add the slices in a single layer, and cook 2‑3 minutes per side until golden.
  • Oven‑Bake – Spread slices on a parchment‑lined sheet, spray lightly with oil, and bake at 425°F for 12‑15 minutes, flipping halfway.
  • Gratin – Layer slices in a buttered dish, pour over cream and cheese, and bake until bubbling and browned.

Because the slices are so thin, they cook quickly and evenly, giving you crisp edges and tender interiors without the guesswork of thicker cuts.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Mandoline

After a successful session, proper cleaning extends the life of your Mandoline Slicer. Disassemble the blade according to the manufacturer’s instructions, rinse under warm water, and dry completely before re‑assembling. Avoid soaking the blade for long periods; stainless steel stays sharp longer when kept dry.

Store the mandoline in a protective case or slip a blade guard over the cutting edge. This prevents accidental damage and keeps the blade ready for your next potato‑thin adventure.

FAQ

Can I use a mandoline for sweet potatoes as well?

Yes. Sweet potatoes are firmer than regular potatoes, so you may need to set the mandoline to a slightly thicker setting (2 mm) and apply a bit more pressure. The hand guard remains essential for safety.

Do I need to oil the mandoline before slicing?

No. The mandoline’s stainless‑steel blade is designed to cut cleanly without oil. Adding oil can make the blade slippery and increase the risk of slipping.

What’s the best way to store sliced potatoes before cooking?

Lay the slices in a single layer on a paper towel, cover with another towel, and keep them in the refrigerator for up to 2 hours. This prevents them from turning brown and maintains crispness.
